newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Merchant said seeking diamond deal for Angola foes.
newsitem.headline: Merchant said seeking diamond deal for Angola foes.

text.p: A powerful diamond merchant, Maurice Tempelsman, is trying to broker a deal between the Angolan government and the UNITA opposition over lucrative diamond areas, analysts and officials said on Friday.
"Tempelsman is working hard to try to convince (UNITA leader Jonas) Savimbi to sign off on a diamond agreement," one diamond analyst told Reuters.
"Of course he has his own interests in mind too," said the analyst, "but apparently he is doing this, in part, on behalf of the American government. They want to see a deal made."

Diplomats and officials close to Angola's peace process have long said that a deal dividing up Angola's diamond fields and ensuring UNITA a fixed income is a key to establishing lasting peace in the war-torn country.
The government and UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, signed a peace agreement in 1994 after 20 years of war.
Though the former rebels are part of a unity government, they still control vast areas of the countryside and up to $700 million of Angola's estimated $1 billion annual diamond production.
Tempelsman, a U.S. citizen who runs the company Lazare Kaplan International which has a number of diamond buying offices in Angola, arrived in Luanda early in the week.
Diplomats say he met Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and later travelled to the central highlands city of Bailundo for meetings with Savimbi.
A U.S. embassy official denied Tempelsman was working on behalf of Washington in trying to bring about a diamond deal.

"Mr. Tempelsman is a private businessman, he is here conducting his own business," said the embassy official. "I can tell you that he is not involved in any sort of U.S. initiative to bring about a diamond deal."
Tempelsman was not available for comment.

Heightened military activity in Angola, including an army offensive against UNITA in the north east, has prompted officials close to the peace process and diplomats to express fears the country is in danger of falling back into war.
A diamond deal, they say, could go far in averting a return to military confrontation.
"At this point it looks like we are going down a road to war," said one diplomat. "There are a couple of escape routes. A diamond deal especially could calm things and allow UNITA a way out."
